replacement: [Footnote B: An opponent, whose intellectual and moral fairness it is a pleasure to acknowledge (the Rev. J. Llewellyn Davis), has objected to this passage. He says, "Surely the rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much upon the motive with which it is done. Suppose that a tyrant, when his enemy jumped into the sea to escape from him, saved him from drowning simply in order that he might inflict upon him more exquisite tortures, would it tend to clearness to speak of that rescue as 'a morally right action?' Or suppose again, according to one of the stock illustrations of ethical inquiries, that a man betrayed a trust received from a friend, because the discharge of it would fatally injure that friend himself or some one belonging to him, would utilitarianism compel one to call the betrayal 'a crime' as much as if it had been done from the meanest motive?" I submit that the man who saves another from drowning in order to kill him by torture afterward does not differ from the man who does the same thing from duty or benevolence in motive only. The act itself is different. In the case supposed, the rescue is only the necessary first step of an act far more atrocious than leaving him to drown would have been. Suppose Mr. Davis had said, "The rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much" — not upon the motive, but — "upon the _intention_." No utilitarian would have differed from him. Through an oversight too common not to be quite venial, Mr. Davis has in this case confounded the very different ideas of Motive and Intention. There is no point that utilitarian thinkers (and Bentham pre-eminently) have taken more pains to illustrate. The morality of the action depends entirely on the intention, that is, on what the agent _wills to do_. But the motive, that is, the feeling that makes him will so to do, makes no difference in the morality when it makes none in the act. It does make a great difference in our moral estimation of the agent, especially if it indicates a good or a bad habitual _disposition_, a bent of character from which useful actions, or hurtful ones, are likely to arise.]
